title: Κορώνη καὶ κύων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 171. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κορώνη Ἀθηνᾷ θύουσα κύνα ἐφ’ ἑστίασιν ἐκάλεσεν.
sentences.tr: Korōnē Athēnāi thyousa kyna eph’ hestiasin ekalesen.
sentences.l: A crow, sacrificing to Athena, invited a dog to a feast.
sentences.n: The god receiving a sacrifice stands in the dative, Ἀθηνᾷ; ἐπί with the accusative gives the purpose one is invited for. A Greek sacrifice ended in a meal, so the invitation follows from the offering as a matter of course.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἔφη πρὸς αὐτήν· « Τί μάτην τὰς θυσίας ἀναλίσκεις ; ἡ γὰρ δαίμων οὕτως σε μισεῖ ὡς καὶ τῶν σῶν οἰωνῶν τὴν πίστιν περιελέσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Ho de ephē pros autēn· « Ti matēn tas thysias analiskeis ; hē gar daimōn houtōs se misei hōs kai tōn sōn oiōnōn tēn pistin perielesthai. »
sentences.l: And he said to her: « Why do you spend your sacrifices in vain ? For the goddess so hates you as even to take away the credit of your omens. »
sentences.i: And he said to her: « Why waste your sacrifices ? The goddess hates you so much that she has stripped your omens of all credit. »
sentences.n: δαίμων is of either gender, and the feminine article ἡ is what marks the divinity here as Athena rather than some god at large. οὕτως … ὡς with an infinitive is the regular result construction — "so much that". περιελέσθαι, aorist middle of περιαιρέω, is to strip a thing off all round. τὴν πίστιν is the credit a sign is given, the willingness to trust it: the crow's cries are still heard, but no one reads anything in them.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ κορώνη ἀπεκρίνατο· « Ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο αὐτῇ θύω, διότι οἶδα αὐτὴν ἀπεχθῶς διακειμένην, ἵνα διαλλαγῇ. »
sentences.tr: Kai hē korōnē apekrinato· « Alla kai dia touto autēi thyō, dioti oida autēn apechthōs diakeimenēn, hina diallagēi. »
sentences.l: And the crow answered: « But for this very reason I sacrifice to her, because I know her to be hostilely disposed, so that she may be reconciled. »
sentences.i: And the crow answered: « But that is the very reason I sacrifice to her — because I know she is ill-disposed toward me, so that she may be reconciled. »
sentences.n: οἶδα takes a supplementary participle for what one knows to be the case (αὐτὴν … διακειμένην), where a verb of saying would take an infinitive. διάκειμαι with an adverb is Greek's ordinary way of saying what state a person is in, and does duty as the passive of διατίθημι: ἀπεχθῶς διακειμένην, "in a state of hostility". ἵνα διαλλαγῇ is a purpose clause with the aorist passive subjunctive of διαλλάσσω, "be reconciled".

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοὶ διὰ φόβον τοὺς ἐχθροὺς εὐεργετεῖν οὐκ ὀκνοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō polloi dia phobon tous echthrous euergetein ouk oknousin.
sentences.l: Thus many, out of fear, do not shrink from doing good to their enemies.
sentences.n: ὀκνέω with an infinitive is to hang back from doing a thing, so οὐκ ὀκνοῦσιν is understatement: not that they merely consent, but that nothing holds them back at all. The motive left standing is φόβος, where affection would be expected.
